title: The Frost Reaches the Heart

pages.text:
*The Bearer's Almanac, Entry 19: Every gift is a loan.*

The hatch was a trap.

Wen kicked it open, but the air that rushed up was not the cool night breeze of the harbor. It was the stale, dusty heat of a cellar that had been sealed for years. Behind them, the soldiers were already on the deck, the sound of their boots on the wood creating an urgent rhythm that matched the frantic beating of her own pulse.

"Behind you!" Shen Yu shouted.

Wen spun around. Three soldiers stood at the far end of the warehouse, their spears leveled. They were not looking at Shen Yu. They were looking at her hands.

"Move," the lead soldier said, his voice bored and professional. "Do not make a scene. The Guild prefers order."

Mo stepped between the soldiers and Wen, raising her pole as if it were the only thing in the world she trusted. "You will not take her," Mo said. "She is not cargo."

"Everything is cargo," the soldier replied. "Even water."

Wen did not think. Thinking took time, and time was a luxury the river no longer afforded anyone. She reached out with her hands, not to the soldiers, but to the air around them. She felt the dampness on the walls, the condensation on the wooden beams, the heavy moisture in the breath of every person in the room. It was not much water, just the memory of rain, but it was hers to move.

She pulled.

The moisture in the air rushed toward her outstretched palms, gathering and thickening until it turned from mist into a solid, shimmering wall of ice. The temperature in the warehouse dropped sharply, and the soldiers gasped, their breath pluming in white clouds.

But the cost came with the ice.

It started at her fingertips, a sharp, biting cold that felt like a burn. It raced up her wrists, her forearms, her elbows. She tried to pull it back, to release the ice, but the connection was already made. The cold was not just a sensation; it was a presence, sliding into her blood and settling in her bones.

She looked at her hands. The skin was pale, translucent, almost blue. And then she looked up, and her eyes caught the reflection in the polished surface of a nearby metal table.

Her ponytail was white.

Not a streak. Not a hint. The entire length of her black hair, from the roots at her scalp to the tips where the blue cloth was tied, had turned the color of fresh snow. The blue cloth looked like a bruise against the stark whiteness.

Wen stared at her reflection. The face looking back was hers, but the eyes were wide and terrified, and the skin was so pale it seemed to have no color at all. She was becoming something else. Something cold.

The ice wall shattered. The soldiers scrambled back, knocking over crates. In the chaos, Mo grabbed Shen Yu’s arm and pulled him toward the broken hatch.

"Go," Wen said. Her voice was thin and reedy. "Now."
pages.image: Wen stands in a dim warehouse, her entire black ponytail turned stark white, hands outstretched, shards of ice floating around her, three soldiers recoiling in the background, Mo and Shen Yu running toward a dark hatch.

pages.text:
They were in a small, cramped room beneath the warehouse, lit by a single tallow candle. The air was thick with the smell of damp wood and old oil. Shen Yu was shaking. His hands were wrapped around his surveyor’s staff, his knuckles white, his glasses fogged with his own breath.

"It is written," he said. His voice was high, tight. "In the oldest river-office scroll I have ever read. The one from the first dynasty. It says... it says the power does not come from the water. It comes from the bearer."

Wen sat on a crate, her legs pulled up to her chest. She was shivering, not from the cold, though she was cold, but from the vibration of her own limbs. "That is not possible," she said. "Water is external. I move it. I do not give it."

"You give it your warmth," Shen Yu said. He took off his glasses and wiped them on his vest. "That is the trade. The energy required to move mass against gravity, against flow, it has to come from somewhere. It comes from your body heat. Your life force."

Mo said nothing. She was standing by the door, watching the shadows. But Wen could feel her presence, a solid, warm anchor in the room.

"Then why does it stop?" Wen asked. "Why did the river stop?"

"Because the bearer is gone," Shen Yu said. "Or frozen. The scroll says that if the frost reaches the heart, the bearer turns to ice. They do not die. They are... preserved. Kept in the cold place, where the river begins."

Wen looked at her hands. The white frost was still there, faintly visible on her fingertips, like a dusting of sugar. "My mother," she said. The words felt heavy, clumsy in her mouth. "She went to the glacier. I thought she was lost. I thought she died."

"She did not die," Shen Yu said. "She was kept. Like a seed in winter soil. Waiting for spring."

The candle flame flickered. For a moment, the shadows in the room seemed to stretch, to reach for them. Wen looked at Mo. Mo’s face was calm, but her eyes were wet.

"Is it true?" Wen asked. "About the heart?"

Mo nodded. "It is true," she said. "I have seen it. I have seen what the frost does. It takes the warmth, and it leaves the shape. And the shape remembers."

Wen closed her eyes. She could feel the cold in her chest, a dull, spreading ache. It was not pain. It was a slowing. A quieting. As if the world was becoming very far away, and very bright, and very still.
pages.image: Shen Yu, wearing round glasses and a brown vest, speaks urgently to Wen, who sits on a crate looking pale, Mo stands by the door with a bamboo pole, a single candle flickers in the dim room.

pages.text:
Wen did not cry. The cold had drawn the moisture from her eyes, leaving them dry and bright, while she sat perfectly still with her hands intertwined in her lap, counting the slow, deliberate beats of her own heart against the silence of the room.

"She did not leave me," Wen said, her voice flat and stripped of all usual urgency. "I used to think she abandoned me out of anger, or that I was simply not enough for her to keep."

Mo crossed the damp floor and sat down beside her without speaking, taking Wen's cold hand in her own weathered grip; the heat from the ferrywoman’s skin seeped into Wen’s frozen fingers like a warm current flowing into a stagnant pool, offering a small, precious comfort that felt almost too good to be true.

"I held her hand," Mo said quietly. "When she went up to the glacier, she was already freezing to the bone. She told me to let go. She said the river needed her, and that the river does not share."

Wen looked at the old woman, her gaze steady. "That is not true. The river shares. It feeds the terraces and fills the pools. It is the most generous thing in this world."

"No," Mo replied, her eyes glistening in the candlelight. "It is the most necessary thing. And necessity is cold."

Wen pulled her hand back, refusing the warmth because she wanted the truth more than she wanted comfort. "If the river needs her, then I need to give it back. Not the water. The cost. The frost."

"You cannot," Shen Yu interrupted, his voice trembling with anxiety. "It is too late. The frost has already reached your chest."

Wen looked down at her hair, where the white was stark and shocking in the amber glow, but beneath that whiteness she could see the faintest hint of black at the roots, a tiny, stubborn thread of life refusing to yield.

"No. It is not too late. It is just expensive."

She stood up, her legs weak but holding her balance as she looked at the two of them, at Mo’s deep worry and Shen Yu’s visible fear, and felt something stir in her chest that was not warmth but a sharp, clear resolve.

"We have to leave. The soldiers will be back, and the river is waiting."

Mo stood up and handed Shen Yu a rolled map. "The outer rafts. There is a boat. It is small, but it is fast. And it is empty."

"Empty?" Shen Yu asked, his eyes widening behind his fogged glasses.

"No," Mo said, her voice firm and final. "It is ready."
pages.image: Mo sits next to Wen, holding her hand, Wen looks pale with white hair, Shen Yu stands holding a map, the candlelight casts long shadows on the wooden walls.

pages.text:
The skiff was a narrow sliver of hull, painted the same dull grey as the wooden pilings that held the raft-town together, designed to vanish against the dark timber. It hung from a post at the edge of the platform, rocking gently in the black water, while the air grew heavy with the sharp, stinging smell of tar and the sweet rot of old fish.

"Quickly," Mo said, her hands working the knots with the speed of long habit. "The current is strong tonight. If we catch the ebb, we can be past the town before the soldiers find the gap."

Wen stepped into the boat. It listed sharply under her weight, a gentle, reassuring tilt that reminded her she was solid, not liquid. She settled into the center, crossing her legs, and forced her hands to remain still at her sides. She did not reach for the water. She did not try to push the current. She knew, with a certainty that felt like a physical weight, that if she used her power now, the frost would finish the job. She would become ice. She would join her mother in the cold, and the river would be free, but she would be gone.

"So we row?" Shen Yu asked. He was already in the stern, his surveyor’s staff tucked tight under his arm, his eyes darting to Wen as if waiting for her to perform some impossible feat.

"We row," Wen said. "And we think."

Mo began to row. Her strokes were strong, steady, rhythmic, pulling the boat forward with a mechanical grace that required no magic and no cost. The water pushed against the sides of the hull, lifting it, carrying it, a simple and human effort that felt like the only honest thing left in the world.

They slipped out from under the shadow of the great lanterns of Floating Lantern Town. The lights above them were a sea of gold and red, reflecting in the dark water, while the town itself became a maze of wood and rope, a floating city that seemed to breathe and shift with the tide.

"Stars," Shen Yu said, looking up with a sudden, quiet wonder. "I can see the stars. The cloud layer must have broken."

He pulled out his compass, then stopped, his fingers hovering over the glass. He looked at the sky, at the pinpricks of light scattered across the blackness, and tilted his head. "The North Star," he said. "It is there. Just above the lanterns. I can steer by it."

"Can you?" Wen asked.

"I am a surveyor," Shen Yu said, adjusting his glasses against the damp air. "I measure things. Stars are just very far away points. I can measure them."

Mo smiled, a small and tired expression that was entirely real. "Then you steer, Shen Yu. And I will row. And you, Wen Lan, you just have to stay warm."

Wen looked at her hands. The frost was still there, a fine white powder on her fingertips, but it was not spreading. She was still herself. She was still warm.

"I will try," she said.

The boat moved faster, the lights of the town blurring into a streak of color, then fading into the darkness. They were alone on the water, moving toward the mountains.
pages.image: A small grey skiff moves through dark water, Mo rows at the back, Shen Yu looks up at the stars, Wen sits in the center looking forward, the lights of Floating Lantern Town blur in the background.

pages.text:
The town fell away behind them, its lanterns shrinking from a blazing sea to a single amber smear, and finally to a memory. The water changed its character as they passed the last stilt house. It lost the sluggish, tar-heavy drag of the harbor and gained the crisp, metallic snap of a mountain stream. It smelled of wet granite and cold pine needles, a scent that cut through the stale air of the raft docks with the sharpness of a freshly split bamboo.

They had reached the fresh river.

It ran thin and bright through the darkness, a silver vein pulsing under the moon. The water was not the dead, cracked mud of Hollow Pool, nor was it the measured, rationed cups from the cisterns of the White Basin. It moved with a wild, untamed purpose, swirling over submerged stones in patterns that no engineer had drawn. It was simply water, doing what water does when it has nowhere to be captured.

Wen looked down at her reflection in the churning surface. Her hair, once a solid mass of white frost, was softening now. The moonlight caught the tips, but near her scalp, faint dark lines were returning, like ink bleeding back into paper. She was still alive.

She extended her hand toward the current. The water was cold, biting, but it did not freeze. It was clean, rushing over her fingers with a gentle, insistent pressure. It felt like a hand reaching for her, demanding not to be held, but to be acknowledged.

"Then I will not waste what is left," Wen said. Her voice was steady, stripped of the tremor that had plagued her since the salt flats.

She did not lift the water. She did not try to steer it or hold it in a sphere. She let it rush past her fingertips, feeling the sheer volume of it, the kinetic energy that a river of this size possessed. It was a promise. A debt. A life.

Mo stopped rowing. The current took the keel, carrying them forward with a smooth, inexorable glide. Shen Yu lowered his compass, the brass needle swinging wildly in the changing magnetic field of the open water.

"We are going up," Wen said. "To the source. To the glacier. To my mother."

"And then?" Mo asked. Her voice was low, barely audible over the rush of the current.

"And then," Wen said, "we give it back."

The boat moved forward, into the dark, into the cold, into the unknown. The water flowed around them, quiet and strong, carrying them toward the roof of the world.
pages.image: A small boat drifts on a clear, sparkling river at night, Wen touches the water, her white hair glowing, Mo and Shen Yu watch, the dark mountains rise in the background.
